Charlatan

SHAR-luh-tun -- from Italian ciarlatano, related to ciarlare ('to chatter'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Charlatan is a person who falsely claims to have skill or knowledge in order to deceive others.

The 'award-winning wine critic' quoted in every ad turned out to be a charlatan who couldn't tell an expensive vintage from grape juice in a blind taste test.

Worked Example

The 'award-winning investment guru' promised guaranteed forty percent returns every year -- a classic charlatan's pitch aimed at retirees with no financial background to catch the lie.

Notice a charlatan's deception is always about false expertise -- pretending to have real skill, training, or knowledge that they don't actually have. That's different from a demagogue, who deceives a crowd about politics, not personal qualifications.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — ciarl-

root — ciarl-: to chatter, babble (Italian (ciarlare))

Put it together

Put it together: Charlatan comes from an Italian word for someone who chatters or babbles -- picture a fast-talking market peddler shouting about his miracle cure. The word kept that sense of empty, showy talk covering up a total lack of real skill.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: Charlatan is built on the Italian verb ciarlare, 'to chatter or babble' -- the word literally brands a fake expert by his fast, empty sales talk. The insult targets how the phony sounds, not what he sells.

Strength Check

Word Choice

A charlatan deceives people by falsely claiming personal expertise or skill, like a fake doctor or a fake financial guru. Compare Demagogue, who manipulates a crowd's emotions to gain political power, not to sell a false skill. A charlatan's lie is 'trust my expertise'; a demagogue's lie is 'trust me to lead you.'
